question: Tell me about a number you refused to take at face value. What did you find?

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a number you refused to take at face value. What did you find?

Our dashboard showed 92% task completion. I pulled the raw logs because the number felt high compared to what I was seeing in tickets. It turned out the query was counting partial saves as complete, so real completion was 67%. I fixed the query and added a validation step.
What prompted you to check the logs instead of just reporting the 92%?
My manager had asked why velocity looked off, so I wanted to make sure the metric matched what the team actually delivered.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a number you refused to take at face value. What did you find?
Role: new grad on support tooling team
Situation: dashboard showed 92% completion but velocity felt off
Action: pulled raw logs, found partial saves counted as complete
Outcome: corrected to 67%, added validation step
Quote: "I wanted to make sure the metric matched what the team actually delivered."
Follow-up: Asked what prompted the check; candidate tied it to manager feedback on velocity
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Dive Deep. The candidate questioned a completion metric on their own dashboard after noticing a mismatch with observed velocity. They pulled raw logs, discovered partial saves were inflating the number from 67% to 92%, and fixed the query plus added validation. This shows ownership of their own output and willingness to dig when something felt inconsistent. The follow-up confirmed the trigger came from manager feedback rather than external pressure. Biggest strength is treating a single metric as suspect and verifying it at the data level instead of reporting it upward.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a number you refused to take at face value. What did you find?

Our launch readiness score was 88% across three teams. I asked for the underlying incident data because the score didn't match the on-call load we were seeing. It turned out two teams were under-reporting Sev-2s due to a shared ticket template. We aligned the taxonomy and the real readiness dropped to 71%, which changed the launch date.
How did you get the other teams to change their reporting?
I showed them the ticket volume mismatch in a shared doc and let them see the on-call pager data themselves.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a number you refused to take at face value. What did you find?
Role: senior on platform team
Situation: launch readiness score at 88% across three teams
Action: requested incident data, found under-reporting of Sev-2s from shared template
Outcome: corrected to 71%, shifted launch date, aligned taxonomy
Quote: "I showed them the ticket volume mismatch in a shared doc."
Follow-up: Asked how they influenced other teams; candidate described sharing raw pager and ticket data
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Dive Deep. The candidate challenged an 88% readiness score that conflicted with observed on-call load across three teams. They surfaced under-reported Sev-2s caused by a shared ticket template, corrected the figure to 71%, and used the data to influence launch timing. Influence happened by sharing raw pager and ticket evidence rather than authority. The follow-up showed they enabled other teams to reach the same conclusion. Biggest strength is turning a single questionable metric into cross-team process change with measurable impact on a launch decision.

I didn't have time to pull the incidents myself.

The story shows awareness of a potential issue but no follow-through. Biggest gap is stopping at a verbal flag instead of using data to test the number.

raiseTranscript.text: Tell me about a number you refused to take at face value. What did you find?

Our quarterly cost-per-acquisition target looked on track at $42. I asked finance for the cohort-level LTV curves because CAC alone didn't explain why retention was flattening. We discovered the number excluded the top 8% of high-value customers who were being routed through a different attribution path. Adjusting for that showed true blended CAC at $61 and forced us to re-forecast the entire growth plan.
What trade-offs did you surface to the leadership team?
We presented three options: accept lower volume at the real cost, change channel mix, or adjust the profitability target. They chose the channel mix change.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a number you refused to take at face value. What did you find?
Role: VP of Growth
Situation: quarterly CAC target at $42 looked on track
Action: requested cohort LTV curves, found high-value customers excluded from attribution
Outcome: true blended CAC $61, re-forecast growth plan, leadership chose channel mix change
Quote: "We presented three options: accept lower volume at the real cost, change channel mix, or adjust the profitability target."
Follow-up: Asked about trade-offs presented; candidate described three concrete options given to leadership
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Dive Deep. The candidate questioned a $42 CAC figure that appeared on track and requested cohort LTV curves, revealing that high-value customers were excluded from attribution. The corrected blended CAC of $61 triggered a full growth re-forecast. They framed three explicit trade-offs for leadership rather than simply flagging the error. The follow-up confirmed they drove a strategic decision on channel mix. Biggest strength is connecting a single metric discrepancy to org-level planning and forcing a choice among quantified options.

CAC was reported at $42. I asked my team to double-check the spreadsheet and they confirmed the number.
Did the check change any downstream plans?
No, it stayed the same so we kept the original forecast.

exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Dive Deep. The candidate asked their team to verify a $42 CAC figure in the spreadsheet and accepted the confirmation without further scrutiny. No exploration of attribution paths, cohort effects, or LTV linkage occurred. The verification produced no change to the growth forecast. The story remains limited to confirming an existing calculation. Biggest gap is treating verification as a one-time spreadsheet check rather than questioning whether the metric itself captured the right population.
